title: Constitutional Amendment B: 60 Percent Vote for Citizen-Initiated Tax Increases

context.text: Referred by the Utah Legislature as S.J.R. 2 (2025 General Session), which passed the Senate 21-8-0 and the House 55-17-3. It takes effect November 23, 2026 if approved by a majority of those voting, and would apply to initiated legislation subject to a vote after November 1, 2026.
Ballotpedia lists two certified statewide measures in Utah for November 3, 2026.

question.text: Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to require that citizen-proposed laws that increase taxes compared to existing law be approved by at least 60% of voters, instead of a simple majority?

summary.text: Amends Article VI, Section 1 so that a citizen-initiated law must be approved by at least 60% of those voting, rather than a majority, if it imposes a new tax, expands an existing tax to additional items or transactions, increases an existing tax rate, or (for a property tax) lowers the rate by less than it would under current law. The existing two-thirds requirement for initiatives on wildlife taking is unchanged. KUER reports that 60 percent of registered voters is about 1.25 million people, and that 2018 initiatives on Medicaid expansion (53.3%), medical marijuana (52.7%) and Proposition 4 (50.3%) passed with less than 60%. No fiscal estimate was found.

measure.yesMeans: Requires that citizen-initiated laws that create or increase taxes be approved by at least 60% of voters instead of a simple majority.
measure.noMeans: Keeps the simple-majority requirement for all citizen initiatives other than the existing two-thirds requirement for wildlife-taking initiatives.

argumentsFor.text: Republican Rep. Jordan Teuscher said during 2025 House floor debate (quoted by KUER): "This protects the taxpayers, makes sure that they really understand what they're doing as they move forward."

Republican Rep. Casey Snider said on the House floor in 2025 (quoted by KUER) that the higher threshold would protect rural Utahns: "Rural Utah lives in fear of suburbia, and it's not because you're ill-intentioned or anything like that, but it is because there are more of you than there are of us."

argumentsAgainst.text: Elizabeth Rasmussen, executive director of Better Boundaries, said (as quoted by KUER): "They're using taxes kind of as a scare tactic to get people to vote yes, when in reality, it's about consolidating power, making it harder for us to exercise our constitutional right to use ballot initiatives."
Democratic Rep. Doug Owens said, as reported by KUER, that he believed half of Utahns were "as able as 60% to identify a good proposal."

researchNotes: The statewide ballot text is taken from the official county ballot published on the Utah Public Notice Website (the same statewide question appears on every county's ballot); the resolution text and legislative votes come from the Legislature's publication of the proposed amendments. The Lieutenant Governor's online voter information pamphlet (vote.utah.gov) carries the sponsors' and opponents' arguments, but the pamphlet PDF available did not include them, so the arguments below come from KUER's report quoting legislators and advocates on each side; they are not the pamphlet's official arguments. Ballotpedia is cited only for the count of certified statewide measures (two). A veto referendum on congressional boundaries, a public-union collective bargaining referendum and several initiatives are tracked by Ballotpedia as not on the ballot.
